column2: For months the floe drifted north. They hoped it would carry them to Paulet Island, where emergency stores had been left years before.
On the twenty-third of March 1916, through the fog, they saw land. Joinville Island.
But it was out of reach, across broken ice. They were drifting past it, towards the open ocean.
The floe was breaking up around them. On the ninth of April 1916, Shackleton ordered everyone into the three boats.
That night, the floe they camped on split in two, right under a tent. A sailor named Ernest Holness fell into the sea, still in his sleeping bag.
Shackleton reached down and pulled him out. Then the crack opened wider and Shackleton was left alone on the other piece.
The men pushed out a boat and brought him back. Then Shackleton made Holness walk all night, so he would not freeze in his wet clothes.
For almost a week they rowed and sailed between the floes, soaked and freezing, with almost nothing to drink.
On the fifteenth of April 1916, they landed on Elephant Island. It was the first solid ground they had stood on for 497 days.
But nobody would ever look for them here. Elephant Island was empty, far from any shipping route.
